claims.text: A rebuild of every matched function in 16 public decompilations on the released compiler with default settings found 10 of 14 agent-assisted projects hold at 99–100%, while four fall below 99% because they rely on patched compilers or per-file settings. Pokémon Colosseum, a GameCube title, is the worst at 71.4% stock matches, and both human-built references (Melee, The Wind Waker) hit 100%. Headline match numbers therefore overstate genuine source recovery in a minority of agent projects.

Only rebuilding on the stock compiler exposes them, so verification cost is a compute-and-build cost, not a reviewer-time cost.

Existing projects such as Melee keep reporting, but new AI-assisted projects will have no shared independent number, which makes the single-author stock-compiler audit more significant. The searched question (match rates from automated source-variant search on near-miss functions) is not answered by any of these sources.

claims.text: Final code generation takes optimized intermediate code and assigns variables to a small, fixed set of registers, with each intermediate line expanding into one or more machine instructions. Because register assignment and instruction expansion happen at this last stage, a source tweak that leaves the intermediate form unchanged will leave the output unchanged, while one that alters it can reshuffle registers and instruction order.

meta.query: Why does a source-level random mutation change the machine code that the Metrowerks compiler emits for some constructs (register allocation order, instruction scheduling, stack slot layout, loop shape) and leave it unchanged for others, and why can a permuter score of zero still fail to be byte-identical?
meta.capability: You can stop expecting a source-level change to map one-to-one onto machine-code change, and plan any byte-matching or equivalence work around the fact that compilation is a many-line-per-statement translation.

claims.text: Mutation research defines equivalent mutants as variants with identical outputs on all inputs, and notes full equivalence is undecidable and in practice only checked on a finite test suite. Equivalence in behavior says nothing about identical instruction bytes, and that gap is one reason a zero-difference score can still fall short of a byte-exact match.

meta.query: Why does a source-level random mutation change the machine code that the Metrowerks compiler emits for some constructs (register allocation order, instruction scheduling, stack slot layout, loop shape) and leave it unchanged for others, and why can a permuter score of zero still fail to be byte-identical?
meta.capability: You can stop treating a behaviorally equivalent source variant as proof of identical compiled output, and budget effort accordingly when hunting for a variant that reproduces exact bytes.

claims.text: Classical mutation operators were designed to mimic programmer faults, and research notes fixed operator sets are insufficient even for real bugs. Operators like replacing a loop with a single iteration change behavior, so they do not target the output-preserving rewrites needed to nudge compiler output, which means random edits need guidance toward constructs the compiler is sensitive to.

meta.query: Why does a source-level random mutation change the machine code that the Metrowerks compiler emits for some constructs (register allocation order, instruction scheduling, stack slot layout, loop shape) and leave it unchanged for others, and why can a permuter score of zero still fail to be byte-identical?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming the mutation operators used for testing are the right search space for changing compiler output, and avoid relying on the idea that many random edits will eventually find the right one.

claims.text: The documented PowerPC/EABI allocation policy favors caller-save registers and only falls back to callee-save registers when no caller-save is free. So a small source change that adds one more live value, or a call that forces values to survive across it, can push a variable from a caller-save register into a callee-save one, and the compiler then also has to save and restore that register in the prologue and epilogue. This is a general allocator rule, not a Metrowerks-specific finding, so how it applies to Metrowerks is an inference.

meta.query: Why does a small change in how a C function is written cause the Metrowerks PowerPC compiler to assign registers or lay out stack slots differently, even when the resulting instruction sequence looks the same?
meta.capability: You can stop expecting a PowerPC compiler's register choices to follow only from how the source reads, and plan for the compiler's built-in preference order deciding which values survive in which registers.

claims.text: Under the PowerPC EABI, where each argument lives depends on its type and its position in the list: the first 8 integer arguments go in R3 to R10, the first 8 float arguments in F1 to F8, and long integers take aligned register pairs. Extra arguments spill to consecutive stack slots, with floats taking 2 words and aligned. Changing one parameter's type or order can therefore shift every later argument into a different register or stack slot.

meta.query: Why does a small change in how a C function is written cause the Metrowerks PowerPC compiler to assign registers or lay out stack slots differently, even when the resulting instruction sequence looks the same?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that changing a function's parameter or return types is cosmetic, and treat it as something that can reshuffle registers and stack slots for every caller and callee.

claims.text: The verifier project defines a match as requiring four things at once: identical code bytes apart from address fields, references that resolve to the same original targets, matching table contents, and identical unwind and exception-handling metadata. A function that looks identical instruction by instruction can still be reported as different because a referenced constant, vtable, or exception table differs, so 'perfect instruction match' is not the same as 'done'.

meta.query: What happens when a decompiled function scores as a perfect match by instruction, relocation and symbol comparison but the final linked bytes still differ from the original binary, and how often has this been reported?
meta.capability: You can stop treating a function-level match as proof the rebuilt program is the original, and instead insist on checking data, tables and exception metadata as well before declaring a function done.

claims.text: The verifier tolerates certain gaps: without an exported data-item list, a data object is compared only up to the rebuilt object's last nonzero byte, so a table with trailing zero entries or a truncated string still matches. Functions using the newer compressed exception-handling format cannot be verified and are reported as differences, and 32-bit or non-MSVC builds are unsupported. A reported match count can therefore be either overstated or understated depending on setup.

meta.query: What happens when a decompiled function scores as a perfect match by instruction, relocation and symbol comparison but the final linked bytes still differ from the original binary, and how often has this been reported?
meta.capability: You can trust a progress dashboard's match counts only to the extent you know which gaps the checker silently tolerates, and budget review time for those blind spots.

claims.text: The tool keeps a regression list of matched functions and, in check mode, fails the build when any listed function stops matching or when library code is wrongly counted as decompiled. This turns matching progress into a ratchet that can run in continuous integration, rather than a number someone re-measures by hand.

meta.query: What happens when a decompiled function scores as a perfect match by instruction, relocation and symbol comparison but the final linked bytes still differ from the original binary, and how often has this been reported?
meta.capability: You can lock in gains by gating every build on a committed list of already-matched functions, so a regression is caught the moment it happens rather than discovered at final link.

claims.text: The ReCo paper (ACL 2024) reports that having an LLM rewrite the codebase itself to normalize style, in addition to generating example code for the query, boosts retrieval accuracy by up to 35.7% for sparse retrieval, 27.6% for zero-shot dense and 23.6% for fine-tuned dense. The gain comes from closing the stylistic gap between generated and real code. Nothing in the material tests this on mwcc or on older console toolchains, so whether it transfers to compiler-specific matching is unproven.

claims.text: The Code2Code tool indexes 1,100,000+ snippets across 2,400+ repositories but supports only Python, C++, C, PHP, JavaScript, TypeScript, Lua, Go, Java and Rust. It finds code similar in meaning regardless of style, which differs from the exact byte or instruction matching that compiler-specific work needs. It says nothing about mwcc output or optimizer quirks, so it should not be counted on for that use.

claims.text: Macabeus's benchmark of 60 functions from two real projects (Sonic Advance 3 on GBA and Animal Forest on N64, both non-Metrowerks) matched 74% on average across 6 runs using m2c, decomp-permuter and Claude Sonnet 4.6, with 88% of functions giving the same outcome every run. 12 functions always failed, so the ceiling is a stable set of hard functions, not luck. No GameCube/Wii Metrowerks-specific rate was reported in these sources, so applying 74% to Metrowerks code is an extrapolation.

claims.text: Register allocation is an NP-complete problem that compilers solve only approximately, typically via graph coloring with heuristics for spilling and splitting. Because the result depends on heuristic ordering and priority rankings, tiny source changes can flip which values get which registers, so the match is a search over heuristic behavior rather than a deterministic translation.

meta.query: Why do register allocation, instruction scheduling and inlining decisions in the Metrowerks compiler make some functions nearly impossible to match by rewriting source, and how does this differ from GCC-era compilers?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that a hard-to-match function is a matter of finding the right source rewrite, and recognise that register assignment is an approximation the compiler may resolve differently after small source changes.

claims.text: Values with long live ranges and many interfering neighbors (constrained nodes) are the hard cases, forcing spill or split decisions that depend on estimated execution frequency and spill cost. Functions heavy in such values are where small differences in the allocator's cost estimates produce visibly different register assignments and spill code.

meta.capability: You can budget extra time for functions with heavy register pressure or long live ranges, expecting them to be the ones where source rewrites fail to reproduce the target's register choices.
